'''Riazuddin'''{{efn|[[Punjabi language|Punjabi]]/[[Urdu language|Urdu]]: {{nq|ریاض الدین}}<ref name=Tribune>[https://tribune.com.pk/story/602599/obituary-noted-physicist-dies Obituary: Noted physicist dies (Riazuddin)] The Express Tribune (newspaper), Published 10 September 2013, retrieved 7 August 2020</ref><ref name="Qadir2014">{{cite journal|last1=Qadir|first1=Asghar|title=Riazuddin: In Memoriam|journal=Physica Scripta|volume=89|issue=8|year=2014|article-number=080401|issn=0031-8949|doi=10.1088/0031-8949/89/8/080401|bibcode=2014PhyS...89h0401Q|s2cid=121181424 }}</ref>}} (10 November 1930 – 9 September 2013) was a Pakistani [[theoretical physicist]], specialising in [[high-energy physics]] and [[nuclear physics]]. He is considered one of the early pioneers of Pakistan's [[Project-706|nuclear weapons development]] and [[Pakistan and weapons of mass destruction|atomic deterrence development]]. Starting his scientific research in 1958, he served as the director of the Theoretical Physics Group (TPG) of the [[Pakistan Atomic Energy Commission]] (PAEC) from 1974 until 1984. Riazuddin was a pupil of [[Abdus Salam]], a [[Nobel Prize in Physics|Nobel laureate in Physics]].<ref name="IAS Fellows"/>

Riazuddin carried out his research at the [[International Centre for Theoretical Physics]] (ICTP), PAEC, the [[European Organization for Nuclear Research]] (CERN) and [[Daresbury Laboratory]] where he published papers in mathematics and physics. Riazuddin also played an important role in education in Pakistan, contributing to the rise of [[science in Pakistan]]. Riazuddin authored several scientific books on [[particle physics]] and [[quantum mechanics]]. Later in his life, he joined the [[National University of Sciences and Technology, Pakistan|National University of Sciences and Technology]] (NUST) as a visiting professor of theoretical physics.

==Biography==
===Early years===
Riazuddin was born in 1930 into a [[Punjabis|Punjabi]] family in [[Ludhiana]], [[British Punjab]]. After the [[Partition of India]], his family migrated to Pakistan in 1947 and settled in [[Lahore]]. He is the twin brother of physicist [[Fayyazuddin]]. At age 17, Riazuddin attended [[University of the Punjab|Punjab University]], and took his [[Bachelor of Science|BSc (Hons)]] in [[mathematics]] under the supervision of [[Abdus Salam]] in 1951.<ref name="IAS Fellows">{{Cite web
 |last        = Islamic Academy of Sciences
 |first       = IAS
 |title       = Professor Riazuddin
 |work        = IAS Fellows
 |publisher   = Islamic Academy of Sciences
 |date        = 2000
 |url         = http://www.ias-worldwide.org/profiles/prof89.htm
 |access-date  = 7 August 2020
 |archive-url  = https://web.archive.org/web/20130214010730/http://www.ias-worldwide.org/profiles/prof89.htm
 |archive-date = 14 February 2013
}}
</ref> Riazuddin also studied under the supervision of Abdus Salam at the [[Postgraduate education|Postgraduate]] level at Cambridge University.<ref name="King Fahd University of Petroleum and Minerals">{{Cite web
 |title       = Prof. Riazuddin
 |work        = King Fahd University of Petroleum and Minerals
 |publisher   = [[King Fahd University of Petroleum and Minerals]]
 |date        = 1996
 |url         = http://faculty.kfupm.edu.sa/PHYS/khodja/Riazuddin.htm
 |access-date  = 7 August 2020
 |archive-url  = https://web.archive.org/web/20110728064231/http://faculty.kfupm.edu.sa/PHYS/khodja/Riazuddin.htm
 |archive-date = 28 July 2011
}}</ref> As a student of mathematics, he learned the advanced course on [[quantum mechanics]] under Abdus Salam, as he had made the course of quantum mechanics outside the regular curriculum.<ref name=NCP>{{Cite web
  | author =Fayyazuddin
  | title =Prof. Abdus Salam, As I know him
  | work =NCP
  | publisher =National Center for Physics
  | url =http://www.ncp.edu.pk/docs/5PPW/Abdus%20Salam/5PPW-Salam%20Lecture-Fayyazuddin.pdf
  | access-date =2018-08-20
  | archive-date =3 March 2016
  | archive-url =https://web.archive.org/web/20160303173216/http://www.ncp.edu.pk/docs/5PPW/Abdus%20Salam/5PPW-Salam%20Lecture-Fayyazuddin.pdf
  }}</ref> In 1951, Salam funded his scholarship, and helped him gain admission to the graduate school of Punjab University. In 1953, Salam supervised his [[Master of Science|MSc]] in [[applied mathematics]] where his master's dissertation dealt with fundamental concepts of mathematical physics.<ref name="IAS Fellows"/><ref name=NCP/> By the time he published his thesis in 1953, he received a [[Gold medal]] from the Punjab University for post-graduate contributions to physics and mathematics.<ref name="Pakistan Academy of Sciences">{{Cite web
 |last        = (PAS)
 |first       = Pakistan Academy of Sciences
 |author-link  = Pakistan Academy of Sciences
 |title       = Profile of Riazuddin
 |work        = Pakistan Academy of Sciences
 |date        = 1959
 |url         = http://www.paspk.org/fellow8.htm
 |access-date  = 7 August 2020
 |archive-url  = https://web.archive.org/web/20110930045314/http://www.paspk.org/fellow8.htm
 |archive-date = 30 September 2011
}}</ref>

With the help of Salam, Riazuddin went to the United Kingdom on a scholarship and attended [[University of Cambridge]]. At Cambridge, he was awarded his [[Doctor of Philosophy|PhD]] in [[Theoretical physics]] in 1959.<ref name="King Fahd University of Petroleum and Minerals"/> Riazuddin's [[dissertation]] was written on "''Charge Radius of Pion''" which also covered many issues relevant to the field of [[Quantum mechanics|quantum theory]].<ref>{{MathGenealogy|78650}}</ref> Riazuddin returned to Pakistan where he joined Punjab University as an [[associate professor]]. In 1968, Riazuddin was awarded the [[Gold Medal|Gold Medal in Physical Sciences]] for scientists under 40 years of age by the [[Pakistan Academy of Sciences]].<ref name= "Pakistan Academy of Sciences"/>

===Academic career===
Riazuddin had joined Punjab University in 1959 as an associate professor of mathematics.<ref name= "Pakistan Academy of Sciences"/> Four years later, he travelled to the United States for a fellowship awarded by Norman March and [[Michael Duff (physicist)|Michael Duff]].<ref name="IAS Fellows"/> He became a [[research associate]] professor at the [[University of Rochester]] where he stayed until 1965.<ref name="IAS Fellows"/> The same year, he joined the [[University of Pennsylvania]] where he taught physics until 1966.<ref name="IAS Fellows"/> Later, he went to [[Chicago]], Illinois where he joined his twin brother [[Fayyazuddin]], and theoretical physicists Faheem Hussain and Peter Rottoli. Riazuddin joined [[University of Chicago]]'s [[Enrico Fermi Institute]] where they created the "Relativity Group".<ref name= "Riazuddin As I know him"/> In 1968, Riazuddin returned to Pakistan on the request of Salam, and joined [[Quaid-i-Azam University]]'s Institute of Physics.<ref name="Theoretical Physics Group">{{Cite web
  | last =Hussain
  | first =Faheem
  | title =The Theoretical Physics Group (TPG) at Quaid-i-Azam University
  | work =Theoretical Physics Group
  | publisher =[[National Center for Physics]]
  | url =https://docs.google.com/viewer?a=v&q=cache:_zxVBIoycQMJ:sse.lums.edu.pk/documents/opednewsletter2005Jun.pdf+raziuddin+siddiqui+mathematician&hl=en&gl=us&pid=bl&srcid=ADGEESgYbTyvht0QyOGWZ2kdbXbd7vre1P_AjT-VB-1dI_2DpMNOVc-kYrGsCsSaD3Cf__VlHte_0QHWtEbio7zUpY3fLOtNloozbVlqBwjWcq0aNpa0w8_1WTodTwdlgkMe32ddbCUX&sig=AHIEtbRikFdqTrDjlTU14excgkyvm4K4mg
  | access-date =7 August 2020}}</ref> He was the founding director of the Institute of Physics (IP) where he engaged in research on string theory, the theory of relativity, particle physics and nuclear physics.<ref name= "Riazuddin As I know him">Riazuddin, As I know him, Masud Ahmad, tribute papers presented at Center for Advanced Mathematics and Physics of National University of Science and Technology (NUST).</ref><ref name="Theoretical Physics Group"/> Later, the scientists of the Relativity Group at the Enrico Fermi Institute returned to Pakistan on the request of Salam.<ref name="Theoretical Physics Group"/> In 1970, he returned to the United States, where he became professor of mathematics at the [[University of Maryland, College Park|University of Maryland]].<ref name= "Pakistan Academy of Sciences"/> Riazuddin left the United States for Italy as Salam asked him to join the [[International Centre for Theoretical Physics]] in 1970.<ref name= "Pakistan Academy of Sciences"/> He was joined there by other students of Salam, and they created a theoretical physics group at the ICTP. In 1971, Riazuddin traveled to the United Kingdom to join the [[Daresbury Nuclear Physics Laboratory]], where he was joined by Michael Duff.<ref name= "Pakistan Academy of Sciences"/> At Daresbury, he became senior research associate.<ref name= "Pakistan Academy of Sciences"/> There, Riazuddin gained expertise, specialised in nuclear physics, and trained British scientists in the field of nuclear physics.<ref name= "Pakistan Academy of Sciences"/>

In 1981, he became visiting professor of physics and mathematics at the University of Iowa and Virginia Polytechnic Institute and State University, now [[Virginia Tech]].<ref name="IAS Fellows"/> In 1982, Riazuddin came back to Pakistan, where he joined [[Quaid-e-Azam University]] as a professor of theoretical physics.<ref name="IAS Fellows"/> In 1982, Riazuddin also went to [[Saudi Arabia]], where he joined [[King Fahd University of Petroleum and Minerals]] and became chairman of the Department of Mathematics and Statistics and also taught physics at the Department of Physics. In 1983, Riazuddin, along with Asghar Qadir, went to [[Trieste]], Italy, to join the [[International Centre for Theoretical Physics]]. Both scientists joined Salam, and they continued research in their fields. In 1998, Riazuddin left King Fahd University of Petroleum and Minerals and returned to Pakistan to rejoin PAEC.<ref name= "Pakistan Academy of Sciences"/>

===Scientific research===
During his post-graduate research, Riazuddin made contributions to mathematical physics, as he was highly interested in complex [[mathematical series]], and its relation to [[modern physics]]. In 1959, Riazuddin was the first physicist to use the [[dispersion relation]] for [[Compton scattering]] of virtual photons on pions to analyse their charge radius.<ref>
{{Cite journal
  | author = Riazuddin
  | date = 1959
  | title = Charge Radius of Pion
  | journal = [[Physical Review]]
  | volume = 114 | issue = 4 | pages = 1184–1186
  | doi =10.1103/PhysRev.114.1184
|bibcode = 1959PhRv..114.1184R }}</ref> For this contribution, he was awarded the doctorate in physics (theoretical) by Cambridge University. He seldom published papers, preferring long correspondences with his brother Fayyazuddin, mentor Abdus Salam, and colleagues including [[Asghar Qadir]], [[Michael Duff (physicist)|Michael Duff]], and [[Masud Ahmad]]. During the 1960s, he associated himself with complex mathematical applications of nuclear physics. In 1960, Riazuddin used Nucleon-nucleon dispersion relation to discriminate proton-proton scattering in [[pseudoscalar meson]]s.<ref>
{{Cite journal
  | author = Riazuddin
  | date = 1964
  | title = Electromagnetic Violation of Conservation of Vector Current
  | journal = [[Physical Review]]
  | volume = 134 | issue = 1B | pages = 235–239
  | doi =10.1103/PhysRev.134.B235
|bibcode = 1964PhRv..134..235R }}</ref> In 1965, Riazuddin carried out the pioneering work on [[Four-current|vector currents]], in which he showed the discrepancy between [[Muon decay|μ-decay]] and the constant gravity, and the strong interaction renormalisation of the [[Beta decay|Beta (β)-decay]].<ref>
{{Cite journal
  | author = Riazuddin
  | date = 1961
  | title = Low-Energy p-p Scattering Phase Shifts and Dispersion Relations
  | journal = [[Physical Review]]
  | volume = 121 | issue =5  | pages =1509–1512
  | doi =10.1103/PhysRev.121.1509
|bibcode = 1961PhRv..121.1509R }}</ref>

The same year, the [[U.S. Atomic Energy Commission]], partnering with the [[Pakistan Atomic Energy Commission]], sponsored Riazuddin to undertake further research. Along with Munir Ahmad Rashid and Fayyazuddin, Riazuddin realised that the physical baryons are considered broken in [[special unitary group]]s, [[symmetric group]]s and the [[tensor product]].<ref>
{{Cite journal
  | author = Riazuddin
  | date = 1961
  | title = Two Types of Baryons in Broken (SU3)L⊗(SU3)R Symmetry
  | journal = [[Physical Review]]
  | volume = 1140 | issue =6B  | pages =1653–1654
  | doi =10.1103/PhysRev.140.B1653
|bibcode = 1965PhRv..140.1653R | last2 = Fayyazuddin
  | last3 = Rashid
  | first3 = M.
  }}</ref> The relevant papers were submitted at the United States Atomic Energy Commission. In 1967, at the Fermi Institute, Riazuddin, with his brother Fayyazuddin, carried out research in the field of [[current algebra]], where they applied the mathematical framework of current algebra in the applications of [[radiative recombination|radiative decays]] of mesons.<ref>{{Cite journal
  | author = Riazuddin
  | author2 = Fayyazuddin
  | name-list-style = amp
  | date = 1967
  | title =Current Algebra and Radiative Decays of Mesons
  | journal = [[Physical Review]]
  | volume = 18 | issue =17  | pages =715–719
  | doi =10.1103/PhysRevLett.18.715
| bibcode=1967PhRvL..18..715F
}}</ref>

In 1982, Riazuddin and Fayyazuddin published a pioneering work on K mesons. Riazuddin postulated that radioactive decay in K mesons have almost vanished when [[chiral symmetry]] is introduced. After the introduction, the symmetries break the [[Standard Model]] of particle physics, even when the contribution from [[penguin diagrams]] is included.<ref>{{Cite journal
  | author = Riazuddin
  | author2 = Fayyazuddin
  | name-list-style = amp
  | date = 1985
  | title =K2π decays
  | journal = [[Physical Review]]
  | volume =32 | issue =7  | pages =1720–1724
  | doi =10.1103/PhysRevD.32.1720
| pmid = 9956336
 |bibcode = 1985PhRvD..32.1720R }}</ref>

From 1972, Riazuddin made pioneering research on [[neutrinos]]— an elusive particle postulated by [[Wolfgang Pauli]] in 1930. In 1972, Riazuddin and Fayyazuddin were the first to post mathematical frameworks of Current-algebra in neutrino scattering to determine the [[Scale invariance]] of Chiral symmetry breaking the [[Hamiltonian (quantum mechanics)|Hamiltonian Quantum Mechanics]].<ref>{{Cite journal
  | author = Riazuddin
  | author2 = Fayyazuddin
  | name-list-style = amp
  | date = 1985
  | title =K2π decays
  | journal = [[Physical Review]]
  | volume =5 | issue =10  | pages =2641–2649
  | doi =10.1103/PhysRevD.5.2641
|bibcode = 1972PhRvD...5.2641F }}</ref>
In 1987, Riazuddin and Fayyazuddin theorised that it is possible get light-neutrino masses in the range of a few electron volts by equalising the masses of superheavy neutrinos in [[background independence]] (universality).<ref>{{Cite journal
  | author = Riazuddin
  | author2 = Fayyazuddin
  | name-list-style = amp
  | date = 1987
  | title =Neutrino masses and electron–muon–τ-lepton universality
  | journal = [[Physical Review]]
  | volume =35 | issue =7  | pages =2201–2205
  | doi =10.1103/PhysRevD.35.2201
| pmid = 9957909
 |bibcode = 1987PhRvD..35.2201F }}</ref>

In 2000, Riazuddin began his research in the series [[List of unsolved problems in physics|unsolved problems in physics]]. In 2005, at the [[National Center for Physics]] (NCP), Riazuddin presented his papers on neutrinos where he provided the mathematical framework of the neutrinos. Neutrinos have heavier masses but the [[neutrino oscillations]] do not completely identify the overall scale of their exact masses because they are exceedingly tiny. To determine the exact masses, Riazuddin introduced the laws of limits, as he realised there was a limit, to the electron energy [[Astronomical spectroscopy|spectra]] in [[tritium]] [[Beta decay|β-decay]]. In 2007, Riazuddin introduced SU(3) symmetry in the theory of [[double beta decay]]. He postulated the light neutrinos formed a [[triplet state]] in a SU(3) symmetry during the process. In 2008, Riazuddin pointed out that the neutrino mass has μ and τ symmetry and the [[Lepton number]] remains constant, a new type of [[Seesaw mechanism]] is formed, the so-called Riazuddin's Seesaw Model, the [[Dirac equation|Dirac mass]] [[Dirac matrix|matrix]] provided the [[Yukawa coupling]] to follow the [[Majorana fermion]] to satisfy the [[Leptogenesis (physics)|Leptogenesis]] asymmetry. Riazuddin proposed that this interaction can be avoided when two of the heavy right-hand neutrinos are (nearly) degenerate.{{citation needed|date=January 2018}}

In 2009, Riazuddin published a mathematical theory of the [[non-standard model]], and its brief extensions to [[Tau (particle)|τ]] (tau) particles – particles that are similar to electrons with negative electric charge.<ref name="NCP 5th Particle Physics Sypnoisis">{{Cite journal
  | author =Riazuddin
  | title =Non-standard interactions
  | journal =NCP 5th Particle Physics Sypnoisis
  | volume =1
  | issue =1
  | pages =1–25
  | publisher =Riazuddin, Head of High-Energy Theory Group at National Center for Physics
  | location =Islamabad
  | date =2009
  | url =http://www.ncp.edu.pk/docs/snwm/Riazuddin_Non_Standartd_Interaction.pdf
  | access-date =20 March 2011
  | archive-date =3 March 2016
  | archive-url =https://web.archive.org/web/20160303233425/http://www.ncp.edu.pk/docs/snwm/Riazuddin_Non_Standartd_Interaction.pdf
  }}</ref> In an experiment performed at the Synchrotron light source installed at the [[Abdus Salam Centre for Physics|National Center for Physics (NCP)]], now the Abdus Salam Centre for Physics, Riazuddin observed the decay of the Tau particle, in which he theorised that hadronisation [[vector current]]s and [[axial vector]]s can be used to study the implicit properties and functions of hadronic resonances, together with Chiral symmetry.<ref name="NCP 5th Particle Physics Sypnoisis"/> These natural elements can be assigned to the parts' [[Weak neutral current|weak current]] that the strong nuclear interaction conserves.<ref name="NCP 5th Particle Physics Sypnoisis"/> With the introduction of such elementary particles, it became critical to study the particle elements that hold the weak interaction.<ref name="NCP 5th Particle Physics Sypnoisis"/>

==1971 war and atomic bomb project==
During his stay at [[Pakistan Atomic Energy Commission|PAEC]], Riazuddin and Fayyazuddin were central figures of Pakistan's atomic program during the early and critical years. In December 1972, Riazuddin returned to Pakistan on the request of Salam.<ref>{{harvnb|Rahman|1998|pp=30–31}}</ref> Salam asked Riazuddin to report to [[Munir Ahmad Khan]] – chairman of the Pakistan Atomic Energy Commission at that time.<ref>{{harvnb|Rahman|1998|pp=31}}</ref> At PAEC, Salam assigned Riazuddin to his Theoretical Physics Group (TPG).<ref>{{harvnb|Rahman|1998|pp=33}}</ref> The Theoretical Physics Group took research in [[fast neutron calculations]] – how neutrons moved in a nuclear chain reaction – the theory [[Relativity of simultaneity|simultaneity]] — how would fission weapon would detonated from several points at the same point during the detonation process – and hydrodynamics – how the explosion produced by a chain reaction might behave – and what kind of and how much fissile material and reflectors would be used.<ref>{{harvnb|Rahman|1998|pp=35–36}}</ref> Salam had attracted theoretical physicists who worked under Riazuddin despite his younger age. Riazuddin was among the scientists who attended the Multan meeting that was managed by Salam and convened by [[President of Pakistan|Pakistan President]] [[Zulfikar Ali Bhutto]]. After the meeting, Salam took Riazuddin, with Munir Ahmad Khan, to Bhutto's residence in Islamabad where the scientists briefed Bhutto about the development of the nuclear weapons programme.<ref>{{harvnb|Rahman|1998|pp=55–59}}</ref>

Although Salam had traveled to the United States to evade the [[Indo-Pakistani war of 1971]], he returned to Pakistan with stacks of historical books on the [[Manhattan Project]] in December 1971.<ref>{{harvnb|Rahman|1998|pp=38–40}}</ref> In December 1973, the [[University of Maryland]] offered him a fellowship, and on the advice of Salam, Riazuddin went to United States.<ref>{{harvnb|Rahman|1998|pp=39–41}}</ref> There, he became a senior [[research scientist]] at the University of Maryland, and obtained the open-source information on the "[[Manhattan Project]]" from the [[Library of Congress]].<ref name="Rahman 1998 39–40">{{harvnb|Rahman|1998|pp=39–40}}</ref> Riazuddin carefully studied American [[theoretical physicist]] [[J. Robert Oppenheimer]]'s approach to develop the first implosion device, and made further advances on [[Tolman–Oppenheimer–Volkoff limit]], [[Oppenheimer–Phillips process]], [[Born–Oppenheimer approximation]].

After his return from the United States, Riazuddin was inducted into the Pakistan Atomic Energy Commission (PAEC) as [[Chief technical officer|member (technical)]].<ref>{{harvnb|Rahman|1998|pp=75–76}}</ref> In 1974, he began to take research with the TPG, and began one of the pioneering member of the TPG.<ref>{{harvnb|Rahman|1998|pp=51–53}}</ref> In 1973, [[Muhammad Raziuddin Siddiqui|Raziddin Siddiqui]] formed the Mathematical Physics Group (MPG) which closely collaborated with Theoretical Physics Group.<ref>{{harvnb|Rahman|1998|pp=59}}</ref> Riazuddin called his mathematician friend [[Asghar Qadir]], who specialised in [[special relativity]] under Riazuddin and Salam, to join the Mathematical Physics Group. Later in his career, Qadir published a college text book on theory of special relativity. Shortly after the India surprise [[nuclear test]] — [[Pokhran-I]], Munir Ahmad Khan called for a meeting to initiate the work on atomic bomb.<ref>{{harvnb|Rahman|1998|pp=55–56}}</ref> Riazuddin and Salam represented the Theoretical Physics Group (TPG), and it was decided to develop the [[Implosion-type nuclear weapon|implosion method]] for the first device.<ref>{{harvnb|Rahman|1998|pp=50–59}}</ref> During the meeting, the word "[[Atomic bomb|bomb]]" was never used; instead academic scientists preferred to use the scientific research rationale.<ref>{{harvnb|Rahman|1998|pp=17–18}}</ref> The Theoretical Physics Group began its research and directly reported to Abdus Salam.<ref>{{harvnb|Rahman|1998|pp=70–94}}</ref>

In 1977, both MPG and TPG scientists completed the design and calculation of an atomic bomb.<ref>{{harvnb|Rahman|1998|pp=65–66}}</ref> Along with Qadir, Riazuddin continued to develop the theoretical designs of the atomic weapon during 1978.<ref>{{harvnb|Rahman|1998|pp=67}}</ref> In 1982 the PAEC finally developed the device under the leadership of [[Munir Ahmad Khan]].<ref>{{harvnb|Rahman|1998|pp=69–70}}</ref> The PAEC carried out the first cold-test of the TPG's theoretical design by May 1983 at [[Kirana Hills]]. The test teams were headed by [[Ishfaq Ahmad]], a nuclear physicist, and Munir Ahmad Khan supervised the testings.<ref>{{harvnb|Rahman|1998|pp=80–81}}</ref>

Riazuddin later disclosed that he worked as part of the team, under Abdus Salam, that worked on designs for Pakistan's nuclear explosive device. As he explained: "We were the designers of the [[Atomic bomb|bomb]], like the tailor who tells you how much of the material is required to stitch a suit. We had to identify the [[fissile material]], whether to use [[plutonium]] or...[[enriched uranium]], which method of detonation, which explosive, which type of tampers and lenses to use, how material will be compressed, how shock waves will be created, what would be the yield.".<ref>{{Cite conference
 |first        = Rehman
 |last         = Shahid-Ur-
 |author2      = Nuclear Threat Initiative ''(NTI)''
 |author2-link = Nuclear Threat Initiative
 |title        = A Tale of Two Scientists
 |book-title    = Long Road To Chagai
 |pages        = 39–40
 |publisher    = Print Wise Publication
 |date         = 1999
 |location     = [[Islamabad]], [[Pakistan]]
 |url          = http://www.nti.org/e_research/profiles/Pakistan/Nuclear/chronology_1974.html
 |access-date   = 7 August 2020
 |archive-url   = https://web.archive.org/web/20110918040826/http://www.nti.org/e_research/profiles/Pakistan/Nuclear/chronology_1974.html
 |archive-date  = 2011-09-18
}}</ref><ref name="Rahman 1998 39–40"/>

Riazuddin also worked in a [[neutron]] [[particle accelerator]] at PAEC. In 2000, Riazuddin retired from PAEC as a [[Scientist|chief scientist]]. In the same year, he was elected as Fellow of the [[Third World Academy of Sciences]] and Fellow of the [[Islamic World Academy of Sciences (IAS)]]. Riazuddin was also a visiting scientist at [[European Organization for Nuclear Research|CERN]].

==Legacy, awards and recognition==
Riazuddin was an internationally known theoretical physicist. He had made contributions with [[CERN]]'s [[Large Hadron Collider|Large Hadron Collider (LHC)]]. At CERN, he was a widely respected [[physicist|theoretician]].

Riazuddin is the recipient of [[Civil decorations of Pakistan|Pakistan's highest civil awards]]: 
*[[Tamgha-i-Imtiaz]] (Medal of Excellence) in 1980<ref name="IAS Fellows"/>
* [[Sitara-i-Imtiaz]] (Star of Excellence) in 1990<ref name="IAS Fellows"/>
* [[Hilal-i-Imtiaz]] (Crescent of Excellence) in 1999<ref name="IAS Fellows"/> 
* [[UNESCO]] [[Albert Einstein]] Gold Medal for Fundamental Science in 2000<ref name="IAS Fellows"/>
* Fellow of the Islamic Academy of Sciences in November 2000<ref name="IAS Fellows"/>
* Gold Medal for outstanding research work in Physical Sciences by [[Pakistan Academy of Sciences]] in 1979<ref name="IAS Fellows"/>

He is one of the [[:Category:Pakistani scientists|Pakistani scientists]] who were very close to [[Prime Minister of Pakistan|Pakistani Prime Minister]] [[Zulfiqar Ali Bhutto]] and [[Abdus Salam]]. At PAEC, Riazuddin had closely worked with another noted Pakistani [[theoretical physicist]] [[Masud Ahmad]] (late). Later in life, he worked as a professor of [[theoretical physics]] and [[Neutrino|neutrino physics]] at the [[National University of Sciences and Technology, Pakistan|National University of Sciences and Technology]], in [[Islamabad]].

He had also been the director of the [[Riazuddin National Center for Physics]],<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.ictp.it/about-ictp/media-centre/news/news-archive/2005/7/ictp-director-in-pakistan.aspx|title=ICTP Director in Pakistan|publisher=ICTP|date=6 July 2005|website=www.ictp.it|url-status=bot: unknown|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170703144057/https://www.ictp.it/about-ictp/media-centre/news/news-archive/2005/7/ictp-director-in-pakistan.aspx|archive-date=3 July 2017|access-date=7 August 2020}}</ref> also at Quaid-e-Azam University. He was most famous for his TPG Group work Riazuddin and his team of theoretical physicists are widely credited to have developed and designed Pakistan's nuclear weapon devices.

On 26 April 2009, a day-long conference was held in [[Islamabad]] to pay tribute to an eminent [[research scientist]] and [[theoretical physicist]], Riazuddin. The conference was organised by [[National University of Sciences and Technology, Pakistan|National University of Sciences and Technology]] ([[National University of Sciences and Technology, Pakistan|NUST]]) and Riazuddin National Centre for Physics (RNCP). In the conference, [[Masud Ahmad]], who is also the student of his, said:

"''Prof. Riaz always put in his best efforts to obtain original results while working on various issues related to science and technology''".

[[National University of Sciences and Technology, Pakistan|NUST]] Rector, Engr. Muhammad Asghar also paid tributes to him and said:

"''Prof. Riazuddin has a very strong and professional background in the field of [[Physics]]. He achieved many distinctions and awards from national as well as international institutes, which includes [[Tamgha-e-Imtiaz]], [[Sitara-i-Imtiaz]] and [[Hilal-e-Imtiaz]] and awards from [[UNESCO]], [[Economic Cooperation Organization]] and [[COMSTECH]] Prize in Physics''".<ref name="IAS Fellows"/>
